content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has emphasized the importance of caregiving interventions to support early childhood development (ECD) during the first three years of life. Approximately 250 million children globally are at risk of not reaching their developmental potential within the first five years of life. Policies and programs that empower caregivers to foster young children’s development are critical. Evidence published in The Lancet in 2017 highlights the significance of nurturing care, which includes practices related to health, nutrition, safety, security, responsive caregiving, and early learning opportunities that promote healthy child development. The health sector plays a pivotal role in delivering nurturing care interventions and has the potential to strengthen this approach through health services and partnerships with other sectors. To guide the health sector, WHO aims to develop evidence-based guidelines to improve ECD, enabling member states to make informed decisions about policies and programs that align with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) related to health, learning, and behavior. These guidelines will complement existing WHO tools and recommendations relevant to nurturing care. A Guideline Development Group (GDG), comprising experts in ECD and health, identified four key research questions to inform recommendations on early learning and responsive caregiving. These questions address the effectiveness of: 1. Responsive caregiving interventions on ECD during the first three years of life. 2. Caregiving interventions that promote early learning on ECD during the first three years of life. 3. Caregiving interventions that support healthy socio-emotional and behavioral development on ECD during the first three years of life. 4. Combined caregiving and nutrition programs on ECD and child growth outcomes during the first three years of life. A fifth question was addressed in a separate review. Across the four original questions, 67 studies (77 records) were reviewed, with outcomes assessed including ECD, attachment, child behavior, growth, health, nutrition, caregiving knowledge, caregiver-child interactions, and caregivers’ mental health. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Final recommendations will be determined by the GDG, informed by evidence-to-decision tables. The nurturing care concept emphasizes caregiving practices such as caregiver sensitivity to children’s physical and emotional needs, protection from harm, opportunities for exploration and learning, and interactions that are responsive, emotionally supportive, and cognitively stimulating. While all sectors have roles in promoting nurturing care, the health sector is particularly important during the first three years of life, a critical period for brain development. WHO’s guidelines aim to improve ECD by identifying effective interventions, feasible delivery approaches, and consolidating WHO-recommended strategies to promote ECD. The target audience includes health managers, workers, development agencies, implementing partners, NGOs, and policymakers in maternal and child health. The guidelines will be developed following the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The systematic review supporting these guidelines assessed evidence for six research questions (four original and two additional analyses) using the PICO (Population/Problem, Intervention, Comparison/Control, Outcome) framework. The review included studies evaluating interventions targeting children and caregivers from pregnancy through the first three years of life, with at least one ECD outcome assessed. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were prioritized, and the risk of bias was evaluated based on factors such as randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and outcome reporting. The review process involved comprehensive literature searches across multiple databases, including PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane CENTRAL, with input from research librarians. The findings will inform WHO’s evidence-based recommendations to support ECD globally.
